verses.text: Solomon son of David secured his rule. The LORD his God was with him and made him very great.
Solomon addressed all Israel, including the commanders of thousands and hundreds, the judges, and every leader in Israel who headed a family.
Then Solomon and the whole assembly went to the high place at Gibeon. God's Tent of Meeting was there, the one the LORD's servant Moses had made in the wilderness.
David had brought God's ark up from Kiriath Jearim to the place he had prepared for it. He had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem.
The bronze altar made by Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, was there in front of the LORD's tabernacle. Solomon and the assembly went there to seek guidance.
Solomon went up to the bronze altar before the LORD at the Tent of Meeting and presented a thousand burnt offerings on it.
That night God appeared to Solomon and said, "Ask me for whatever you want me to give you."
Solomon said to God, "You've shown great faithful love to my father David and made me king in his place.
Now, LORD God, let your promise to my father David stand. You've made me king over people as numerous as the dust of the earth.
Give me wisdom and knowledge so I can lead these people. Who else could govern this great people of yours?"

God told Solomon, "This is what you wanted in your heart. You could have asked for riches, wealth, honor, the lives of those who hate you, or a long life for yourself. You asked instead for wisdom and knowledge to govern the people I've made you king over.
So I'll give you wisdom and knowledge. I'll also give you riches, wealth, and honor beyond what any king before you had or any king after you will have."
Solomon left the high place at Gibeon, where the Tent of Meeting stood, and returned to Jerusalem. He ruled over Israel.
Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen: fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. He stationed them in the chariot cities and with him in Jerusalem.
The king made silver and gold as common as stones in Jerusalem, and cedar as plentiful as the sycamore trees in the lowlands.
Solomon got his horses from Egypt and Kue. The king's traders bought horses in Kue.
They brought chariots and horses from Egypt and sold them for six hundred pieces of silver a chariot and a hundred fifty a horse. They also supplied the Hittite and Syrian kings.
Solomon decided to build a house in honor of the LORD's name and a palace for his kingdom.
He assigned seventy thousand men to haul materials, eighty thousand to cut stone in the mountains, and thirty-six hundred to supervise them.
Solomon sent this message to King Huram of Tyre: "Please do for me what you did for my father David when you sent him cedar to build a house to live in.

I'm about to build a house for the name of the LORD my God and dedicate it to him. We'll burn fragrant incense before him, keep the sacred bread on display, and present burnt offerings morning and evening, on Sabbaths, at new moons, and at the appointed festivals of the LORD our God. This is a lasting requirement for Israel.
The house I'm building will be great because our God is greater than all gods.
But who could build a house that holds him when even the highest heavens can't contain him? Who am I to build him a house except as a place to burn incense before him?

Send me someone skilled in working with gold, silver, bronze, iron, and purple, crimson, and blue fabric, who also knows how to engrave. He'll work with the skilled craftsmen in Judah and Jerusalem whom my father David provided.
Send me cedar, cypress, and algum timber from Lebanon as well. I know your workers know how to cut timber there. My workers will work alongside yours
to prepare plenty of timber for me, because the house I'm about to build will be great and wonderful.
I'll give your woodcutters twenty thousand cors of crushed wheat, twenty thousand baths of barley, twenty thousand baths of wine, and twenty thousand baths of oil."
King Huram of Tyre sent Solomon a written reply: "The LORD made you king because he loves his people."

Huram went on, "Praise the LORD, the God of Israel, who made heaven and earth. He gave King David a wise son with good judgment and understanding who will build a house for the LORD and a palace for his kingdom.
I'm sending Huram-abi, a skilled craftsman with good understanding.

His mother is from the tribe of Dan and his father is from Tyre. He can work with gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, wood, purple and blue fabric, fine linen, and crimson fabric. He can do any kind of engraving and work out any design. Give him a place among your craftsmen and those who served my lord David, your father.
Please send your workers the wheat, barley, oil, and wine you mentioned.
We'll cut as much timber from Lebanon as you need and float it by sea on rafts to Joppa. You can take it up from there to Jerusalem."
Solomon counted all the foreigners living in Israel, following the census his father David had taken. They numbered a hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred.
He assigned seventy thousand to haul materials, eighty thousand to cut stone in the mountains, and thirty-six hundred supervisors to assign the people their work.

Solomon began building the LORD's house in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to his father David. Solomon prepared the site David had chosen, the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
He began building on the second day of the second month in the fourth year of his reign.
Solomon laid the foundation for God's house sixty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, using the old standard for the cubit.
The entrance porch stretched across the full width of the house, twenty cubits. It was a hundred twenty cubits high. Solomon covered the inside with pure gold.
He put a cypress ceiling in the main room, covered it with fine gold, and decorated it with palm trees and chains.
He decorated the house with precious stones. The gold came from Parvaim.
He covered the house with gold, including its beams, thresholds, walls, and doors, and carved cherubim on the walls.
He made the Most Holy Place twenty cubits long, matching the width of the house, and twenty cubits wide. He covered it with six hundred talents of fine gold.
The nails weighed fifty shekels of gold. He covered the upper rooms with gold as well.
He had two cherubim carved for the Most Holy Place, and they covered them with gold.
The cherubim's wings spanned twenty cubits altogether. One wing of the first cherub reached five cubits to the wall, and its other wing reached five cubits to the other cherub's wing.
One wing of the second cherub reached five cubits to the opposite wall, and its other wing reached five cubits to meet the wing of the first cherub.
The cherubim stood on their feet, facing the main room, with their wings spread across twenty cubits.
Solomon made the curtain from blue, purple, and crimson material and fine linen, and decorated it with cherubim.
He also made two pillars thirty-five cubits high in front of the house. Each had a capital five cubits high.
He made chains in the inner sanctuary and put them on top of the pillars. He made a hundred pomegranates and attached them to the chains.
He set up both pillars in front of the temple. He named the one on the right Jachin and the one on the left Boaz.
Solomon made a bronze altar twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and ten cubits high.
He also cast the large basin called the Sea. It was round, ten cubits across, five cubits high, and thirty cubits around.
Two rows of figures shaped like oxen circled under its rim, ten to a cubit. They were cast in one piece with the Sea.
The Sea rested on twelve oxen. Three faced north, three west, three south, and three east. Their hindquarters all faced inward.
The basin was a handbreadth thick, with a rim shaped like the rim of a cup and flared like a lily blossom. It could hold three thousand baths.
Solomon also made ten washbasins, five on the right and five on the left. The bowls were used to rinse what was needed for burnt offerings, and the priests used the Sea to wash themselves.
He made ten gold lampstands according to their prescribed design. He put five on the right side of the temple and five on the left.
He also made ten tables and put five on each side of the temple. He made a hundred gold basins.
He built the priests' courtyard and the large courtyard, made doors for the courtyards, and covered the doors with bronze.
He placed the Sea to the right of the temple, on its southeast side.
Huram made the pots, shovels, and basins. This completed his work for King Solomon on God's house:
two pillars with bowl-shaped capitals on top, and two networks to cover the rounded capitals at the tops of the pillars,
plus four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, with two rows on each network covering the bowl-shaped capitals.
He also made the stands and the basins that rested on them,
the Sea, and the twelve oxen that supported it.
Huram-abi made the pots, shovels, forks, and all the utensils for King Solomon to use in the LORD's house, all from polished bronze.
The king had them cast in clay ground in the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zeredah.
Solomon made so many of these objects that no one could determine the weight of the bronze.
Solomon also made all the furnishings for God's house: the gold altar, the tables for the bread set before God,
and the lampstands with their lamps, all of pure gold, to burn as prescribed in front of the inner sanctuary.
The floral decorations, lamps, and tongs were made of the purest gold.
The snuffers, basins, spoons, and fire pans were made of pure gold. The inner doors to the Most Holy Place and the doors to the temple's main hall were gold as well.
When Solomon finished all the work on the LORD's house, he brought in everything his father David had dedicated. He put the silver, gold, and all the vessels in the treasuries of God's house.
Then Solomon called the elders of Israel and all the tribal and family leaders to Jerusalem to bring the ark of the LORD's covenant up from Zion, the City of David.
All the men of Israel gathered with the king for the festival in the seventh month.
When all Israel's elders had arrived, the Levites lifted the ark.
The Levitical priests brought up the ark, the Tent of Meeting, and all the sacred vessels that had been kept in the tent.
King Solomon and the whole assembly of Israel gathered before the ark and sacrificed more sheep and cattle than anyone could count.
The priests brought the ark of the LORD's covenant to its place in the inner sanctuary of the temple, the Most Holy Place, under the wings of the cherubim.
The cherubim's wings spread out over the ark, covering both the ark and its carrying poles from above.
The poles were long enough that their ends could be seen from just outside the inner sanctuary, but they couldn't be seen from outside the temple. The ark is still there today.
The ark held only the two tablets Moses had put there at Horeb, when the LORD made a covenant with the Israelites after they came out of Egypt.
The priests came out of the holy place. All the priests who were there had consecrated themselves, regardless of which division they belonged to.

All the Levite singers were there: Asaph, Heman, Jeduthun, and their sons and brothers. Dressed in fine linen, they stood east of the altar with cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps. A hundred twenty priests stood with them, blowing trumpets.

The trumpeters and singers joined in one sound to thank and praise the LORD. They raised their voices with trumpets, cymbals, and other instruments, praising the LORD: "He is good. His faithful love lasts forever!" Then a cloud filled the LORD's house.
The priests couldn't stand up to serve because of the cloud. The glory of the LORD filled God's house.
Then Solomon said, "The LORD said he would live in thick darkness.
And I've built you a house to call home, a place where you can live forever."
The king turned to face the whole assembly of Israel and blessed them as they stood.
He said, "Praise the LORD, the God of Israel. He kept with his own hands the promise he spoke to my father David:
'Since the day I brought my people out of Egypt, I hadn't chosen any city from Israel's tribes for a house to bear my name, or anyone to rule over my people Israel.
Now I've chosen Jerusalem for my name to be there, and I've chosen David to lead my people Israel.'
My father David wanted to build a house to honor the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
The LORD told my father, 'It was good that you wanted to build a house to honor my name.
But your own son will be the one to build the house for my name.'
The LORD has done what he promised. I've succeeded my father David and taken Israel's throne, as the LORD said, and I've built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
I've placed the ark there. It holds the covenant the LORD made with the Israelites."
Solomon stood in front of the LORD's altar before the whole assembly of Israel and spread out his hands.

He had made a bronze platform five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high and set it in the middle of the courtyard. He stood on it, then knelt in front of the whole assembly and stretched his hands toward heaven.
He said, "LORD, God of Israel, there is no god like you in heaven or on earth. You keep your covenant and show faithful love to your servants who live before you wholeheartedly.
You kept the promise you made to your servant David, my father. You spoke it with your mouth, and what we see today you fulfilled with your hand.

Now, LORD, God of Israel, keep this promise to your servant David, my father: 'You will always have a descendant before me on Israel's throne, as long as your children pay attention to how they live and follow my law as you have lived before me.'
Now, LORD, God of Israel, let the word you spoke to your servant David come true.
Will God really live here on earth with people? Even the highest heavens can't hold you, much less this house I've built.
Still, LORD my God, pay attention to your servant's prayer and plea. Listen to the cry and prayer I'm bringing before you.
Keep your eyes on this house day and night, on the place where you said you would put your name. Hear the prayers your servant makes toward this place.
Hear the pleas of your servant and your people Israel when they pray toward this place. Hear them from your home in heaven, and when you hear, forgive.
If someone wrongs a neighbor and is required to swear an oath, and they come before your altar in this house to swear it,
hear from heaven and act. Judge between your servants, making the guilty answer for what they've done and giving the innocent the justice they deserve.
If your people Israel are defeated by an enemy because they've sinned against you, and they turn back, confess your name, and pray and plead before you in this house,
hear from heaven, forgive your people Israel's sin, and bring them back to the land you gave them and their ancestors.
When the sky shuts and there is no rain because they've sinned against you, if they pray toward this place, confess your name, and turn from their sin when you discipline them,
hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel. Teach them the good way to live and send rain on the land you gave your people as their inheritance.
If famine or disease strikes the land, or blight, mildew, locusts, or caterpillars come, or enemies surround their cities, whatever plague or sickness comes,
hear any prayer or plea from one person or from all your people Israel. Each one knows their own pain and trouble, and they spread their hands toward this house.
Hear from heaven, where you live, and forgive. Give each person what their conduct deserves, for you know their heart. You alone know every human heart.
Then they'll honor you with reverence and live in your ways as long as they live in the land you gave our ancestors.
As for a foreigner who doesn't belong to your people Israel, when they come from a distant country because of your great name, your mighty hand, and your outstretched arm, and pray toward this house,
hear from your home in heaven and do what they ask, so all the peoples of the earth may know your name and revere you as Israel does. Let them know this house I've built bears your name.
When your people go out to fight their enemies wherever you send them and pray toward this city you've chosen and this house I've built for your name,
hear their prayers and pleas from heaven, and uphold their cause.
If they sin against you, as everyone does, and in your anger you give them over to enemies who take them captive to a land far away or nearby,
and they come to their senses in the land where they're held captive and turn back and plead with you there, saying, 'We've sinned, we've done wrong, and we've acted wickedly,'
if they return to you with all their heart and soul in the land of their captivity, and pray toward the land you gave their ancestors, the city you've chosen, and the house I've built for your name,
hear their prayers and pleas from your dwelling in heaven. Uphold their cause, and forgive your people who have sinned against you.
Now, my God, please keep your eyes open and your ears attentive to the prayers made in this place.
Rise, LORD God, and come to your resting place, you and the ark of your strength. LORD God, may your priests be clothed with salvation, and may your faithful people rejoice in your goodness.
LORD God, please welcome the one you've anointed. Remember the faithful love you showed David your servant."
When Solomon finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices. The LORD's glory filled the temple.
The priests couldn't enter the LORD's house because his glory filled it.

All the Israelites saw the fire come down and the LORD's glory rest on the temple. They bowed with their faces to the pavement, worshiped, and thanked the LORD, saying, "He is good. His faithful love lasts forever!"
Then the king and all the people brought sacrifices before the LORD.
King Solomon sacrificed twenty-two thousand head of cattle and a hundred twenty thousand sheep. This is how the king and all the people dedicated God's house.

The priests took their places, and the Levites stood with the instruments King David had made for praising and thanking the LORD. David had used their music to praise the LORD with the words, "His faithful love lasts forever." The priests blew their trumpets opposite the Levites, and all Israel stood.

Solomon set apart the middle of the courtyard in front of the LORD's house. He offered the burnt offerings and the fat of the peace offerings there because the bronze altar he had made was too small to hold the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and fat.
Solomon kept the festival for seven days with all Israel. A huge crowd came from as far as the entrance of Hamath in the north and the brook of Egypt in the south.
On the eighth day they held a solemn assembly. They had spent seven days dedicating the altar and seven days celebrating the festival.
On the twenty-third day of the seventh month, Solomon sent the people home. They were joyful and glad for the kindness the LORD had shown to David, to Solomon, and to his people Israel.
Solomon finished the LORD's house and the royal palace. He completed everything he had planned for the LORD's house and his own house.
Then the LORD appeared to Solomon at night and said, "I've heard your prayer and chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice.
If I shut the sky so no rain falls, or command locusts to eat up the land, or send disease among my people,
and my people who bear my name humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn away from their wicked ways, I'll hear from heaven. I'll forgive their sin and heal their land.
My eyes will be open and my ears attentive to prayers offered in this place.
I've chosen this house and made it holy so that my name will be there forever. My eyes and my heart will always be there.
As for you, if you live before me as your father David did, do everything I've commanded you, and keep my statutes and rulings,
I'll establish your royal throne, just as I promised your father David when I said, 'You will always have a descendant to rule Israel.'
But if you turn away and abandon the statutes and commands I've given you, and go serve and worship other gods,
I'll uproot my people from the land I gave them. I'll cast this house out of my sight, even though I set it apart for my name. I'll make it an object of ridicule among all peoples.
Everyone who passes this once imposing house will be shocked and ask, 'Why has the LORD done this to this land and this house?'

People will answer, 'They abandoned the LORD, the God of their ancestors, who brought them out of Egypt. They turned to other gods and worshiped and served them. That's why the LORD brought all this disaster on them.'"
Solomon spent twenty years building the LORD's house and his own palace.
Afterward, he rebuilt the towns Huram had given him and settled Israelites there.
Solomon went to Hamath Zobah and took control of it.
He built Tadmor in the wilderness and all the storage towns in Hamath.
He rebuilt Upper Beth Horon and Lower Beth Horon as fortified towns with walls, gates, and bars.
He also built Baalath, all his storage towns, towns for his chariots and horsemen, and whatever else he wanted to build in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and throughout the land he ruled.
People still lived in the land from the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, all peoples outside Israel.
Solomon forced their descendants, whom the Israelites had left alive in the land, to work for him. Their forced labor continues to this day.
Solomon used Israelites as soldiers, senior commanders, and officers over his chariots and horsemen, and exempted them from forced labor on his projects.
King Solomon had two hundred fifty chief officers who supervised the people.

Solomon moved Pharaoh's daughter from the City of David to the house he had built for her. He said, "My wife must live elsewhere than in the house of David king of Israel, because every place the LORD's ark has entered is holy."
Then Solomon presented burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar he had built in front of the temple porch.
He offered them as required each day and followed Moses' command for Sabbaths, new moons, and the three yearly festivals: Unleavened Bread, Weeks, and Booths.

Following his father David's instructions, Solomon appointed the divisions of priests to serve and the Levites to lead praise and assist the priests in their daily duties. He assigned gatekeepers by division to each gate, as David the man of God had commanded.
The priests and Levites followed the king's instructions in every matter, including the care of the treasuries.
Solomon's work on the LORD's house was carried through from the day its foundation was laid until it was finished. The LORD's house was complete.
Then Solomon went to Ezion Geber and Eloth, on the coast of Edom.
Through his officials, Huram sent Solomon ships and experienced sailors. They sailed with Solomon's servants to Ophir and brought back four hundred fifty talents of gold for King Solomon.

When the queen of Sheba heard how famous Solomon was, she traveled to Jerusalem to test him with difficult questions. She came with a huge caravan, including camels carrying spices, large amounts of gold, and precious stones. When she met Solomon, she spoke to him about everything on her mind.
Solomon answered every question she asked. Nothing was too difficult for him to explain.
The queen of Sheba saw Solomon's wisdom and the palace he had built.

She saw the food at his table, how his servants were seated, how his attendants served and dressed, his cupbearers and their clothing, and the stairway by which he went up to the LORD's house. It took her breath away.
She told the king, "What I heard back home about what you've done and how wise you are was true.
I had to come and see for myself before I believed it. I wasn't told even half of how great your wisdom is. You've surpassed everything I heard about you.
How fortunate your people are, and how fortunate these servants are to stand before you all the time and hear your wisdom.

Praise the LORD your God, who delighted in you and put you on his throne to rule for him. Because your God loves Israel and wants them to stand forever, he made you their king to uphold justice and do what is right."
She gave the king a hundred twenty talents of gold, a great quantity of spices, and precious stones. Spices like the ones the queen of Sheba gave King Solomon had never been seen there before.
The servants of Huram and Solomon who brought gold from Ophir also brought algum timber and precious stones.
The king used the algum wood for terraces at the LORD's house and at the royal palace, and for harps and stringed instruments for the singers. Nothing like these had been seen in Judah before.
King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba whatever she wanted and asked for, more than she had brought him. Then she and her servants went back to her own country.
In one year Solomon received six hundred sixty-six talents of gold,
besides what came in from traders and merchants. The kings of Arabia and the governors of the land also brought Solomon gold and silver.
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of hammered gold, using six hundred shekels of gold for each one.
He made three hundred smaller shields of hammered gold, using three hundred shekels for each. He put the shields in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
The king also made a large ivory throne and covered it with pure gold.
The throne had six steps and an attached gold footstool. There were armrests on both sides of the seat, with a lion standing beside each armrest.
Twelve lions stood along the six steps, one on either side of each step. No other kingdom had made anything like it.
All King Solomon's drinking vessels were gold, and all the vessels in the House of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. Silver wasn't considered valuable in Solomon's time.
The king's ships sailed to Tarshish with Huram's servants. Once every three years they returned with gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in wealth and wisdom.
Kings from all over the earth sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom God had given him.
Year after year they each brought tribute: silver and gold vessels, clothing, armor, spices, horses, and mules.
Solomon had four thousand stalls for horses and chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. He stationed them in the chariot cities and with him in Jerusalem.
He ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt.
The king made silver as common as stones in Jerusalem and cedar as plentiful as the sycamore trees in the lowlands.
Horses were brought to Solomon from Egypt and from lands all around.

The rest of what Solomon did, from beginning to end, is written in the history of Nathan the prophet, the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and the visions of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat.
Solomon ruled all Israel from Jerusalem for forty years.
Solomon died and was buried in the city of his father David. His son Rehoboam became king in his place.
Rehoboam went to Shechem because all Israel had gathered there to make him king.
Jeroboam son of Nebat had fled to Egypt to escape King Solomon. When he heard what had happened, he came back from Egypt.
The people sent for him, and Jeroboam came with all Israel to speak to Rehoboam. They said,
"Your father put a heavy yoke on us. Lighten the hard labor and the heavy burden he laid on us, and we'll serve you."
He told them, "Come back in three days." So the people left.
King Rehoboam asked the elders who had advised his father Solomon during his lifetime, "How do you think I should answer these people?"
They answered, "If you're kind to these people, give them what they're asking for, and speak well to them, they'll serve you forever."
But Rehoboam set their advice aside and consulted the young men who had grown up with him and now served him.
He asked them, "What do you think we should tell these people who say, 'Lighten the yoke your father put on us'?"
The young men who had grown up with him said, "These people told you, 'Your father put a heavy yoke on us. Make it lighter.' Tell them, 'My little finger is thicker than my father's waist.
My father laid a heavy yoke on you, and I'll make it even heavier. My father punished you with whips, and I'll punish you with scorpions.'"
So Jeroboam and all the people came back to Rehoboam on the third day, as the king had told them to do.
King Rehoboam answered them harshly and ignored the elders' advice.
He said what the young men had advised: "My father put a heavy yoke on you. I'll make it even heavier. My father punished you with whips, and I'll punish you with scorpions."
The king refused to listen to the people. God brought this about so that the LORD would fulfill what he had told Jeroboam son of Nebat through Ahijah the Shilonite.

When all Israel saw that the king would ignore them, they answered him, "What share do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. Back to your tents, Israel! Look after your own house, David!" Then the Israelites went home.
Rehoboam continued to rule the Israelites who lived in the towns of Judah.
King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, the supervisor of forced labor, but the Israelites stoned him to death. The king hurried into his chariot and fled to Jerusalem.
Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David ever since.
When Rehoboam reached Jerusalem, he gathered a hundred eighty thousand handpicked warriors from Judah and Benjamin to fight Israel and win the kingdom back for himself.
But the LORD gave this message to Shemaiah, the man of God:
"Speak to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the Israelites in Judah and Benjamin.
Tell them, 'The LORD says: Don't march out to fight your own people. Everyone go home, because I brought this about.'" They listened to the LORD and turned back instead of marching against Jeroboam.
Rehoboam stayed in Jerusalem and built up the defenses of towns in Judah.
He built up Bethlehem, Etam, and Tekoa,
as well as Beth Zur, Soco, and Adullam,
Gath, Mareshah, and Ziph,
Adoraim, Lachish, and Azekah,
and Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron. These were fortified towns in Judah and Benjamin.
He strengthened the strongholds, appointed commanders, and stocked them with food, oil, and wine.
He made every town very strong and supplied it with shields and spears. Judah and Benjamin were under his rule.
The priests and Levites from every part of Israel sided with Rehoboam.
The Levites left their pasturelands and property and moved to Judah and Jerusalem. Jeroboam and his sons had barred them from serving as priests to the LORD.
Jeroboam appointed his own priests for the high places and for the goat and calf idols he had made.
After the Levites came people from every tribe of Israel who had set their hearts on seeking the LORD, the God of Israel. They came to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
They strengthened the kingdom of Judah and supported Rehoboam son of Solomon for three years. During those three years they followed the ways of David and Solomon.
Rehoboam married Mahalath, daughter of Jerimoth son of David and Abihail daughter of Eliab son of Jesse.
Mahalath bore him three sons: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.
Then he married Maacah, Absalom's granddaughter. She bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.
Rehoboam loved Maacah, Absalom's granddaughter, more than all his other wives and concubines. He had eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and he fathered twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters.
Rehoboam made Maacah's son Abijah the leader among his brothers because he intended to make him king.
He acted wisely by sending some of his sons throughout Judah and Benjamin to the fortified towns. He gave them plenty of provisions and sought many wives for them.
Once Rehoboam had secured his kingdom and become strong, he abandoned the LORD's law, and all Israel followed him.
In Rehoboam's fifth year as king, King Shishak of Egypt marched against Jerusalem because the people had been unfaithful to the LORD.
Shishak brought twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen. The troops who came with him from Egypt were too many to count, including Libyans, Sukkiim, and Ethiopians.
He captured Judah's fortified towns and reached Jerusalem.

Shemaiah the prophet went to Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah, who had gathered in Jerusalem because of Shishak. He told them, "The LORD says, 'You abandoned me, so I've left you in Shishak's hands.'"
The leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, "The LORD is right."
When the LORD saw they had humbled themselves, he told Shemaiah, "They've humbled themselves, so I'll spare them and give them some relief. I won't pour out my anger on Jerusalem through Shishak.
They'll still have to serve him, so they can learn what it's like to serve me and what it's like to serve the kingdoms of other lands."
King Shishak of Egypt came up against Jerusalem and carried away the treasures of the LORD's house and the royal palace. He took everything, including the gold shields Solomon had made.
King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace them and entrusted them to the captains guarding the entrance to the royal palace.
Whenever the king went into the LORD's house, the guards carried the shields and then returned them to the guardroom.
Because Rehoboam humbled himself, the LORD turned his anger away and spared him from complete destruction. There were still some good things in Judah.

King Rehoboam strengthened his position in Jerusalem and continued to reign. He was forty-one when he became king and ruled seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the LORD chose out of all Israel's tribes to bear his name. His mother was Naamah the Ammonite.
He did evil because he never set his heart on seeking the LORD.
Rehoboam's deeds, from beginning to end, are recorded in the histories of Shemaiah the prophet and Iddo the seer, in the genealogical records. Rehoboam and Jeroboam were continually at war.
Rehoboam died and was buried in the City of David, and his son Abijah became king in his place.
Abijah became king of Judah in the eighteenth year of Jeroboam's reign.
He ruled in Jerusalem for three years. His mother was Micaiah daughter of Uriel from Gibeah. Abijah and Jeroboam went to war.
Abijah went into battle with four hundred thousand handpicked warriors. Jeroboam lined up against him with eight hundred thousand handpicked fighting men.
Abijah stood on Mount Zemaraim in the hill country of Ephraim and called out, "Listen to me, Jeroboam and all Israel!
Surely you know that the LORD, the God of Israel, gave David and his descendants the right to rule Israel forever through a covenant of salt.
Yet Jeroboam son of Nebat, who served David's son Solomon, rose up and rebelled against his master.
A gang of troublemakers and wicked men rallied to him and overpowered Solomon's son Rehoboam. Rehoboam was young and inexperienced, and he couldn't stand up to them.
Now you plan to stand against the LORD's kingdom, which he entrusted to David's descendants. You've brought a huge army and the gold calves Jeroboam made to be your gods.

Didn't you drive out the LORD's priests, Aaron's descendants, along with the Levites? Then you appointed your own priests the way other nations do. Anyone who comes with a young bull and seven rams to consecrate himself can become a priest of things that aren't gods.
The LORD is our God, and we've stayed with him. The priests who serve the LORD are Aaron's descendants, and the Levites do the work assigned to them.

Every morning and evening they present burnt offerings and fragrant incense to the LORD. They set out the sacred bread on the pure table and tend the lamps on the gold lampstand so they burn every evening. We follow the instructions of the LORD our God, and you've abandoned him.
Look, God is with us at our head. His priests are here with their trumpets to sound the alarm against you. Israelites, don't fight against the LORD, the God of your ancestors. You won't succeed."
But Jeroboam sent men around to lie in wait behind Judah. His main army was in front, and the ambush was behind them.
When the men of Judah looked back, they saw they had enemies in front of them and behind them. They cried out to the LORD, and the priests blew the trumpets.
The men of Judah shouted. As they shouted, God struck down Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah.
The Israelites fled from Judah, and God handed them over.
Abijah and his troops inflicted heavy losses. Five hundred thousand of Israel's chosen men fell in battle.
Israel was subdued that day, and Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
Abijah pursued Jeroboam and captured Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron, along with the villages belonging to each town.
Jeroboam never recovered his strength during Abijah's lifetime. The LORD struck him, and he died.
Abijah grew powerful. He married fourteen wives and fathered twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.
The rest of Abijah's deeds, how he lived and what he said, are recorded in the commentary of Iddo the prophet.
Abijah died and was buried in the City of David. His son Asa became king in his place, and the land had peace for ten years.
Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God.
He removed the altars to foreign gods and the high places, smashed the sacred pillars, and cut down the Asherah poles.
He told Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their ancestors, and to follow his law and commands.
He removed the high places and the sun images from every town in Judah, and the kingdom was at peace under his rule.
Asa built fortified towns in Judah because the land was at peace. He had no wars during those years because the LORD had given him rest.

He told the people of Judah, "Let's build up these towns and surround them with walls, towers, gates, and bars. The land is still ours because we've sought the LORD our God. We looked to him, and he's given us peace on every side." So they built and prospered.

Asa had an army of three hundred thousand from Judah armed with small shields and spears, and two hundred eighty thousand from Benjamin armed with shields and bows. All of them were courageous warriors.
Zerah the Ethiopian marched against them with a million troops and three hundred chariots, and reached Mareshah.
Asa went out to meet him, and they took up their positions in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah.

Asa called to the LORD his God, "LORD, you're the only one who can help when the powerful come against the powerless. Help us, LORD our God. We're relying on you, and in your name we've come to face this huge army. LORD, you are our God. Don't let any human prevail against you."
The LORD struck the Ethiopians before Asa and Judah, and the Ethiopians fled.
Asa and his men pursued them as far as Gerar. So many Ethiopians fell that they couldn't regroup. They were crushed before the LORD and his army. Judah's troops carried off a great deal of plunder.
They struck all the towns around Gerar because terror of the LORD had fallen on them. They plundered the towns, which had plenty to take.
They also struck the camps of the herders and took many sheep and camels. Then they returned to Jerusalem.
God's Spirit came upon Azariah son of Oded.

He went out to meet Asa and said, "Listen to me, Asa and everyone in Judah and Benjamin! The LORD is with you as long as you stay with him. If you seek him, you'll find him. If you abandon him, he'll abandon you.
For a long time Israel lived without the true God, without a priest to teach them, and without the law.
But when trouble came, they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought him, and they found him.
In those days it wasn't safe to come or go. Everyone in the surrounding lands faced serious trouble.
Nation fought nation and town fought town, tearing one another apart, because God troubled them with hardships of every kind.
But you, stay strong and keep working, because your work will be rewarded."

When Asa heard these words and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage. He removed the detestable idols from Judah, Benjamin, and the towns he'd captured in the hill country of Ephraim. He restored the LORD's altar in front of the temple porch.

Then he gathered all Judah and Benjamin, along with the people from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who were living among them. Many had come to him from Israel because they saw that the LORD his God was with him.
They gathered in Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year of Asa's reign.
That day they sacrificed to the LORD seven hundred cattle and seven thousand sheep from the plunder they'd brought back.
They made a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their ancestors, with all their heart and all their soul.
Anyone who refused to seek the LORD, the God of Israel, was to be put to death, regardless of rank or whether they were a man or a woman.
They pledged themselves to the LORD out loud, with shouting and the sound of trumpets and horns.
All Judah celebrated the oath because they'd sworn it wholeheartedly and sought the LORD with everything they had. They found him, and the LORD gave them peace on every side.
King Asa also removed his mother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she'd made a detestable image for Asherah. He cut it down, ground it to dust, and burned it by the Kidron Brook.
The high places remained in Israel, but Asa stayed wholeheartedly devoted all his life.
He brought into God's house the silver, gold, and vessels that he and his father had dedicated.
There was no more war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa's reign.
In the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign, King Baasha of Israel marched against Judah and fortified Ramah to block people from coming to or going from Asa, king of Judah.
Asa took silver and gold from the treasuries of the LORD's house and the royal palace. He sent them to King Ben Hadad of Syria, who lived in Damascus, with this message:
"Let's make a treaty, like the one our fathers had. I've sent you silver and gold. Break your treaty with King Baasha of Israel so he'll pull back from me."
Ben Hadad agreed to King Asa's request and sent his commanders against the towns of Israel. They attacked Ijon, Dan, Abel Maim, and all the storage towns of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard about it, he abandoned the work at Ramah.
King Asa called out all Judah to haul away the stone and timber Baasha had used at Ramah. Asa used those materials to build up Geba and Mizpah.
At that time Hanani the seer went to Asa, king of Judah, and said, "Because you relied on the king of Syria instead of the LORD your God, the Syrian king's army slipped out of your hands.
Didn't the Ethiopians and Libyans come with a huge army, with chariots and more horsemen than you could count? Because you relied on the LORD, he handed them over to you.
The LORD looks throughout the whole earth to show his strength on behalf of those whose hearts are fully devoted to him. You've acted foolishly in this, and from now on you'll face wars."
Asa was furious with the seer over what he had said and threw him in prison. At the same time Asa mistreated some of his people.
Asa's deeds, from beginning to end, are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.
In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa developed a severe disease in his feet. Even as the disease got worse, he turned to his physicians alone and never sought the LORD.
Asa died in the forty-first year of his reign.
They buried him in the tomb he'd cut for himself in the City of David. They laid him on a bier filled with fragrant spices blended by perfumers and lit a very large fire in his honor.
Asa's son Jehoshaphat became king in his place and strengthened his defenses against Israel.
He stationed troops in all the fortified towns of Judah and placed garrisons throughout Judah and in the towns in Ephraim that his father Asa had captured.
The LORD was with Jehoshaphat because he followed the example of his ancestor David's early years and kept away from the Baals.
He sought the God of his father and followed God's commands, turning away from the practices of Israel.
So the LORD secured the kingdom under him. All Judah brought tribute to Jehoshaphat, and he gained great wealth and honor.
He took heart in following the LORD's ways and removed the high places and Asherah poles from Judah.
In the third year of his reign, he sent his officials Ben Hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah to teach in the towns of Judah.
He sent the Levites Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tobadonijah with them, along with the priests Elishama and Jehoram.
They carried the Book of the LORD's Law with them and went through every town in Judah, teaching the people.
Fear of the LORD came over all the kingdoms surrounding Judah, so they left Jehoshaphat alone and made no war on him.
Some Philistines brought Jehoshaphat gifts and silver as tribute. The Arabians brought him flocks, seven thousand seven hundred rams and the same number of male goats.
Jehoshaphat grew very powerful. He built fortresses and storage towns in Judah.
He carried out many projects in the towns of Judah and kept brave, experienced soldiers in Jerusalem.
Here is how they were counted by family. From Judah, among the commanders of thousands, Commander Adnah had three hundred thousand courageous warriors.
Next was Commander Jehohanan, with two hundred eighty thousand men.
Next was Amasiah son of Zichri, who had volunteered to serve the LORD. He had two hundred thousand courageous warriors.
From Benjamin came Eliada, a courageous warrior, with two hundred thousand men armed with bows and shields.
Next was Jehozabad, with a hundred eighty thousand men equipped and ready for war.
These men served the king in addition to the troops he had stationed in fortified towns all across Judah.
Jehoshaphat had great wealth and honor, and he made an alliance with Ahab.
A few years later he went down to visit Ahab in Samaria. Ahab slaughtered plenty of sheep and cattle for Jehoshaphat and the people with him, and persuaded him to go with him to Ramoth Gilead.
King Ahab of Israel asked King Jehoshaphat of Judah, "Will you go with me to Ramoth Gilead?" Jehoshaphat answered, "I'm with you, and my people are with your people. We'll join you in the war."
But Jehoshaphat told the king of Israel, "Please ask the LORD what he has to say first."
The king of Israel gathered four hundred prophets and asked them, "Should we go to war at Ramoth Gilead, or should I hold back?" They said, "Go. God will hand it over to the king."
Jehoshaphat asked, "Is there another prophet of the LORD here we can ask?"

The king of Israel answered, "There's one man we could ask to speak for the LORD, Micaiah son of Imla. I hate him because he always predicts trouble for me and never anything good." Jehoshaphat said, "The king shouldn't talk like that."
So the king of Israel called an officer and said, "Bring Micaiah son of Imla here at once."
The king of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah sat on their thrones in royal robes in the open area at Samaria's gate. All the prophets were prophesying in front of them.
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made iron horns. He said, "The LORD says, 'With these you'll drive back the Syrians until they're wiped out.'"
All the prophets said the same thing: "Attack Ramoth Gilead and you'll succeed. The LORD will hand it over to the king."
The messenger sent to get Micaiah told him, "Look, all the prophets are promising good things to the king. Please agree with them and say something favorable."
Micaiah answered, "As surely as the LORD lives, I'll say whatever my God tells me."
When Micaiah arrived, the king asked him, "Micaiah, should we fight at Ramoth Gilead or should I hold back?" He answered, "Go and succeed. They'll be handed over to you."
The king replied, "How many times must I make you swear to tell me only the truth in the LORD's name?"
Micaiah said, "I saw all Israel scattered across the mountains like sheep without a shepherd. The LORD said, 'These people have no master. Let them each go home in peace.'"
The king of Israel told Jehoshaphat, "Didn't I tell you? He always predicts trouble for me and never anything good."
Micaiah said, "Then hear what the LORD says. I saw the LORD seated on his throne with the whole army of heaven standing to his right and left.
The LORD asked, 'Who will lure King Ahab of Israel into going to Ramoth Gilead, where he'll fall?' One suggested one thing and another suggested something else.
Then a spirit stepped forward, stood before the LORD, and said, 'I'll lure him.' The LORD asked, 'How?'
The spirit said, 'I'll go and put lies in the mouths of all his prophets.' The LORD said, 'You'll lure him and succeed. Go and do it.'
So look, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of these prophets of yours, and the LORD has declared disaster for you."
Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came over and slapped Micaiah across the face. He asked, "Which way did the LORD's Spirit go when he left me to speak to you?"
Micaiah answered, "You'll see on the day you go into an inner room to hide."
The king of Israel ordered, "Take Micaiah back to Amon, the city governor, and to Joash, my son.
Tell them the king says, 'Throw this man in prison and give him only a little bread and water until I return safely.'"
Micaiah said, "If you come back safely at all, the LORD hasn't spoken through me." Then he added, "Everyone, listen to this!"
So the king of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah went up to Ramoth Gilead.
The king of Israel told Jehoshaphat, "I'll go into battle in disguise, and you wear your royal robes." So the king of Israel disguised himself, and they went into battle.
The king of Syria had ordered his chariot commanders, "Fight only the king of Israel. Leave everyone else alone, whatever their rank."
When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "That's the king of Israel!" They turned to attack him. Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him. God drew them away from him.
When the commanders realized he wasn't the king of Israel, they stopped chasing him.
Someone drew his bow at random and hit the king of Israel between the pieces of his armor. The king told his chariot driver, "Turn around and get me out of the battle. I'm badly wounded."
The fighting grew fiercer that day. The king of Israel stayed propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians until evening. Around sunset he died.
King Jehoshaphat of Judah returned safely to his palace in Jerusalem.
Jehu son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and said, "Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? Because you've done this, the LORD is angry with you.
Still, there is good in you. You removed the Asherah poles from the land and set your heart on seeking God."
Jehoshaphat lived in Jerusalem. He went out among his people again, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, and brought them back to the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
He appointed judges throughout the land, in each of Judah's fortified towns.
He told the judges, "Think carefully about what you do. You judge for the LORD himself. He's with you when you give a ruling.
Let reverence for the LORD guide you. Do your work carefully, because the LORD our God deals justly, shows no favoritism, and takes no bribes."
In Jerusalem, Jehoshaphat also appointed some Levites, priests, and Israelite family heads to judge matters concerning the LORD and settle disputes. They returned to Jerusalem.
He gave them these instructions: "Do this work faithfully and wholeheartedly, with reverence for the LORD.

Whenever your people in other towns bring you a case, whether it concerns bloodshed, a law, a command, a statute, or a ruling, warn them so they won't incur guilt before the LORD and bring his anger down on you and your people. Do this and you'll be free of guilt.

Amariah the chief priest will oversee you in everything that concerns the LORD. Zebadiah son of Ishmael, leader of the house of Judah, will oversee everything that concerns the king. The Levites will serve as officers alongside you. Act with courage, and may the LORD be with those who do good."
After this the Moabites, Ammonites, and some of the Meunites came to make war on Jehoshaphat.
Messengers told him, "A huge army is coming against you from Syria, from beyond the sea. They're already at Hazazon Tamar," that is, En Gedi.
Jehoshaphat was alarmed, so he turned to the LORD for help and called for a fast throughout Judah.
People gathered from every town in Judah to ask the LORD for help.
Jehoshaphat stood in front of the new courtyard in the LORD's house, among the people gathered from Judah and Jerusalem.
He said, "LORD, God of our ancestors, aren't you the God in heaven who rules over every kingdom on earth? Power and might are in your hands. No one can stand against you.
Didn't you drive out the people of this land before your people Israel and give it forever to the descendants of Abraham, your friend?
They settled here and built a sanctuary to honor your name. They said,

'If disaster comes on us, whether war, judgment, disease, or famine, we'll stand before this house and before you, because your name is here. We'll cry out to you in our trouble, and you'll hear us and save us.'
Now look at the people of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir. When Israel came out of Egypt, you kept them from invading those lands. Israel went around them and left them alive.
Look how they're repaying us. They've come to drive us out of the land you gave us as our inheritance.
Our God, won't you judge them? We're powerless against this huge army coming at us. We don't know what to do, but our eyes are on you."
All Judah stood before the LORD, with their wives, children, and little ones.
Then the LORD's Spirit came on Jahaziel as he stood in the assembly. He was a Levite from Asaph's family, the son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah.
He said, "Listen, everyone in Judah and Jerusalem, and you too, King Jehoshaphat. The LORD says, 'Don't let this huge army frighten or discourage you. The battle belongs to God.
Tomorrow go down to meet them. They'll be coming up the Pass of Ziz, and you'll find them at the end of the valley in front of the wilderness of Jeruel.

You won't have to fight this battle. Take your positions, stand your ground, and see how the LORD rescues you, Judah and Jerusalem. Don't be afraid or lose heart. Go out to meet them tomorrow. The LORD is with you.'"
Jehoshaphat bowed with his face to the ground, and everyone from Judah and Jerusalem bowed before the LORD and worshiped him.
The Levites from the families of Kohath and Korah stood up and praised the LORD, the God of Israel, with loud voices.

Early the next morning they went out into the wilderness of Tekoa. As they set out, Jehoshaphat stood and said, "Listen to me, Judah and Jerusalem! Trust the LORD your God and you'll stand firm. Trust his prophets and you'll succeed."

After talking it over with the people, he appointed singers to go in front of the army in sacred clothing, praising the LORD with these words: "Give thanks to the LORD, for his faithful love lasts forever."
As they began singing and praising, the LORD set ambushes against the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir who had marched against Judah. They were struck down.
The Ammonites and Moabites turned on the people of Mount Seir and wiped them out. Once they had finished with Seir, they turned on one another.
When Judah reached the lookout over the wilderness, they saw bodies lying on the ground where the huge army had been. No one had escaped.

Jehoshaphat and his people went to collect the plunder. They found valuables everywhere and stripped precious jewels from the dead, more than they could carry. There was so much that it took three days to gather it.
On the fourth day they gathered in the Valley of Beracah and blessed the LORD there. That's why the place is still called the Valley of Beracah.
Then everyone from Judah and Jerusalem returned to Jerusalem with Jehoshaphat leading them. They were joyful because the LORD had given them cause to celebrate over their enemies.
They entered Jerusalem with stringed instruments, harps, and trumpets and went to the LORD's house.
Fear of God came over all the surrounding kingdoms when they heard the LORD had fought against Israel's enemies.
Jehoshaphat's kingdom was at peace because his God gave him rest on every side.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he became king of Judah. He ruled for twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother was Azubah daughter of Shilhi.
He followed the way of his father Asa and kept to it, doing what was right in the LORD's eyes.
The high places remained, though, and the people still hadn't set their hearts on the God of their ancestors.
The rest of what Jehoshaphat did, from first to last, is recorded in the history of Jehu son of Hanani, included in the Book of the Kings of Israel.
After this, King Jehoshaphat of Judah made an alliance with King Ahaziah of Israel, who acted very wickedly.
They joined together to build ships for Tarshish, building them at Ezion Geber.

Then Eliezer son of Dodavahu from Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat: "Because you joined forces with Ahaziah, the LORD has destroyed what you built." The ships were wrecked and couldn't sail to Tarshish.
Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His son Jehoram became king in his place.
Jehoram's brothers were Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah. They were all sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Israel.
Their father had given them generous gifts of silver, gold, and valuables, along with fortified towns in Judah. He gave the kingdom to Jehoram because he was the firstborn.
Once Jehoram had taken over his father's kingdom and made his position secure, he killed all his brothers, along with some of Israel's leaders.
Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for eight years.
He followed the ways of Israel's kings, like the house of Ahab, because he had married Ahab's daughter. He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes.
The LORD spared David's house because of the covenant he had made with David. He had promised David and his descendants that their lamp would always burn.
During Jehoram's reign Edom broke away from Judah and set up a king of its own.
Jehoram went there with his commanders and all his chariots. During the night he attacked the Edomites who had surrounded him, along with their chariot commanders.
Edom has remained in rebellion against Judah ever since. Libnah broke away at the same time because Jehoram had abandoned the LORD, the God of his ancestors.
He built high places in the mountains of Judah and led Jerusalem's people into spiritual unfaithfulness, drawing Judah away from God.
Elijah the prophet sent him a letter: "The LORD, the God of your ancestor David, says, 'You've turned away from the ways of your father Jehoshaphat and of Asa, king of Judah.
You've followed the kings of Israel instead. You've led Judah and Jerusalem into unfaithfulness just as Ahab's house did. You've also killed your own brothers, who were better men than you.
Now the LORD will strike a terrible blow against your people, your children, your wives, and everything you own.
You'll suffer from a severe disease of the intestines that will get worse day after day until your intestines come out.'"
The LORD stirred up the Philistines and the Arabians who lived near the Ethiopians against Jehoram.
They invaded Judah and carried off everything they found in the royal palace, including Jehoram's sons and wives. Only Jehoahaz, his youngest son, was left to him.
After all this, the LORD struck Jehoram with an incurable intestinal disease.
Two years later, his intestines came out because of the disease, and he died in great pain. His people held no funeral fire for him like the ones they had held for his ancestors.
He was thirty-two when he became king and ruled eight years in Jerusalem. He died without anyone mourning his death. They buried him in the City of David, outside the royal tombs.

The people of Jerusalem made Jehoram's youngest son Ahaziah king in his place. The raiding party that came to the camp with the Arabians had killed all his older brothers. So Ahaziah son of Jehoram became king of Judah.
Ahaziah was forty-two years old when he became king and ruled one year in Jerusalem. His mother was Athaliah, a daughter of Omri's family.
He followed the ways of Ahab's house, because his mother advised him to do evil.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, as Ahab's family had done. After his father died, they became his advisers and led him to ruin.
He took their advice and went with King Jehoram son of Ahab of Israel to fight King Hazael of Syria at Ramoth Gilead. The Syrians wounded Jehoram.

Jehoram returned to Jezreel to recover from the wounds he had received at Ramah in the fight against King Hazael of Syria. Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, went down to Jezreel to visit him because he was wounded.
God brought about Ahaziah's downfall through that visit. When Ahaziah arrived, he went out with Jehoram to confront Jehu son of Nimshi, whom the LORD had anointed to wipe out Ahab's house.
While Jehu was carrying out judgment on Ahab's house, he found Judah's officials and the sons of Ahaziah's brothers serving Ahaziah, and he killed them.

Jehu looked for Ahaziah, who was hiding in Samaria. His men caught him, brought him to Jehu, and killed him. They buried him because they said, "He's a descendant of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart." No one from Ahaziah's family had the power to hold the kingdom.
When Ahaziah's mother Athaliah saw that her son was dead, she set out to destroy all the royal descendants of Judah.

But Jehoshabeath, King Jehoram's daughter, secretly took Ahaziah's son Joash away from the royal sons who were being killed and put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Jehoshabeath was Ahaziah's sister and the wife of Jehoiada the priest. She hid Joash from Athaliah and saved his life.
He remained hidden with them in God's house for six years while Athaliah ruled the land.

In the seventh year Jehoiada took courage and made an agreement with the commanders of hundreds: Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zichri.
They went throughout Judah and gathered the Levites from every town, along with the heads of Israel's families. They all came to Jerusalem.
The whole assembly made a covenant with the king in God's house. Jehoiada told them, "Look, the king's son must reign, just as the LORD said about David's descendants.
Here's what you must do. One third of the priests and Levites coming on duty for the Sabbath will guard the entrances.
A third will be at the palace, and a third will be at the Foundation Gate. Everyone else will be in the courtyards of the LORD's house.
Only the priests and Levites on duty may enter the LORD's house. They may enter because they've been set apart as holy. Everyone else must follow the LORD's instructions.
The Levites must surround the king, each with a weapon in his hand. Anyone else who enters the house must be put to death. Stay with the king wherever he goes."

The Levites and all Judah followed Jehoiada the priest's orders. Each commander gathered both the men coming on duty for the Sabbath and the men going off duty, because Jehoiada hadn't dismissed the outgoing shift.
Jehoiada the priest gave the commanders of hundreds the spears and shields that had belonged to King David and were stored in God's house.
He stationed the men with weapons in hand from one side of the house to the other, near the altar and the temple, all around the king.
Then they brought out the king's son, crowned him, gave him the covenant, and made him king. Jehoiada and his sons anointed him and shouted, "Long live the king!"
When Athaliah heard the people running and cheering for the king, she joined the crowd at the LORD's house.

She saw the king standing by his pillar at the entrance, with the commanders and trumpeters beside him. The people celebrated and blew trumpets, and the singers played instruments and led the praise. Athaliah tore her clothes and shouted, "Treason! Treason!"

Jehoiada the priest brought out the army commanders and ordered them, "Take her out between the ranks. Put anyone who follows her to the sword." The priest had told them to spare the LORD's house from her execution.
They cleared a path for her. When she came to the Horse Gate at the palace, they killed her there.
Jehoiada made a covenant with the king and all the people that they would be the LORD's people.
The people went to Baal's temple and tore it down. They smashed his altars and images and killed Mattan, Baal's priest, in front of the altars.

Jehoiada put the LORD's house in the care of the Levitical priests David had assigned to serve there. They were to offer burnt offerings to the LORD as written in Moses' law, with celebration and singing as David had directed.
He stationed gatekeepers at the gates of the LORD's house to keep out anyone who was ceremonially unclean.

Jehoiada gathered the commanders of hundreds, nobles, governors, and all the people of the land and escorted the king down from the LORD's house. They entered the palace through the Upper Gate and seated the king on the royal throne.
All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah had been put to the sword.
Joash was seven years old when he became king and ruled forty years in Jerusalem. His mother was Zibiah from Beersheba.
Joash did what was right in the LORD's eyes throughout the lifetime of Jehoiada the priest.
Jehoiada chose two wives for him, and Joash had sons and daughters.
After some time Joash decided to restore the LORD's house.

He called the priests and Levites together and told them, "Go to the towns of Judah and collect money from all Israel each year to repair the house of your God. Get started right away." But the Levites didn't act quickly.

So the king called for Jehoiada the chief priest and asked him, "Why haven't you made the Levites collect from Judah and Jerusalem the tax that Moses, the LORD's servant, and the assembly of Israel established for the Tent of the Testimony?"
The sons of wicked Athaliah had broken into God's house and given the things dedicated to the LORD's house to the Baals.
At the king's command they made a chest and placed it outside the gate of the LORD's house.
They announced throughout Judah and Jerusalem that the people should bring the LORD the tax Moses, God's servant, had required of Israel in the wilderness.
All the officials and people gladly brought their money and dropped it into the chest until it was full.

Whenever the Levites brought the chest to the king's officials and they saw it held a lot of money, the king's secretary and the chief priest's officer emptied it and returned it to its place. They did this day after day and collected a large sum.
The king and Jehoiada paid the people in charge of the work on the LORD's house. They hired masons and carpenters, as well as ironworkers and bronzeworkers, to repair it.
The workers kept at it, and the repairs moved forward. They restored God's house to its original design and made it strong.

When they finished, they brought the money left over to the king and Jehoiada. It was used to make equipment for the LORD's house, including utensils for service and sacrifices, spoons, and gold and silver vessels. Burnt offerings continued at the LORD's house throughout Jehoiada's lifetime.
Jehoiada lived to a good old age. He was a hundred thirty years old when he died.
They buried him among the kings in the City of David because of the good he had done for Israel, for God, and for God's house.
After Jehoiada died, Judah's leaders came and bowed before the king, and he listened to them.
They abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their ancestors, and worshiped Asherah poles and idols. Their guilt brought God's anger on Judah and Jerusalem.
The LORD sent prophets to bring the people back to him. The prophets warned them, but the people refused to listen.

God's Spirit came upon Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest. He stood above the people and said, "God says, 'Why are you breaking the LORD's commands? That's why you can't succeed. You've abandoned the LORD, and now he's abandoned you.'"
They plotted against him, and on the king's orders they stoned him in the courtyard of the LORD's house.
King Joash forgot the kindness Zechariah's father Jehoiada had shown him and had Zechariah killed. As Zechariah died, he said, "May the LORD see what you've done and repay you for it."
At the turn of the year the Syrian army marched against Joash. They invaded Judah and Jerusalem, killed the leaders of the people, and sent all their plunder to the king of Damascus.

The Syrian army came with only a small force, yet the LORD handed a much larger army over to them because Judah had abandoned the LORD, the God of their ancestors. In this way they brought judgment on Joash.

The Syrians withdrew, leaving Joash badly wounded. His own servants plotted against him because of the blood of Jehoiada the priest's sons, and they killed him in his bed. They buried him in the City of David, outside the royal tombs.
The men who plotted against him were Zabad son of Shimeath the Ammonite woman and Jehozabad son of Shimrith the Moabite woman.
The accounts of his sons, the heavy burdens laid on him, and the rebuilding of God's house are recorded in the commentary on the Book of the Kings. His son Amaziah became king in his place.
Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother was Jehoaddan from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, though his heart wasn't fully in it.
Once his kingdom was secure, he executed the officials who had killed his father, the king.

He spared their children. He followed what the LORD commanded in the Book of Moses: "Parents must never be put to death for their children's sins, or children for their parents' sins. Each person is to die for their own sin."

Amaziah gathered all Judah and Benjamin and organized them by family under commanders of thousands and hundreds. He counted the men twenty years and older and found three hundred thousand handpicked men fit for battle and able to use a spear and shield.
He also hired a hundred thousand proven warriors from Israel for a hundred talents of silver.
A man of God came to him and said, "Your Majesty, don't take Israel's army with you. The LORD isn't with Israel, with any of the people of Ephraim.
If you go, fight with all the strength you have, and God will still bring you down before the enemy. God has the power to help you or bring you down."
Amaziah asked, "What about the hundred talents I already paid the Israelite troops?" The man of God answered, "The LORD can give you much more than that."
So Amaziah dismissed the troops that had come from Ephraim and sent them home. They were furious with Judah and went home in a rage.
Amaziah took courage and led his people to the Valley of Salt, where they struck down ten thousand people from Seir.
The men of Judah took ten thousand alive, brought them to the top of a cliff, and threw them over. They all died on the rocks below.
Meanwhile the soldiers Amaziah had sent home from the battle attacked the towns of Judah from Samaria to Beth Horon. They killed three thousand people and took a great deal of plunder.
When Amaziah came home after defeating the Edomites, he brought back the gods of Seir. He set them up as his own gods, bowed down to them, and burned incense to them.
The LORD was angry with Amaziah and sent a prophet to ask him, "Why are you turning to the gods of people those gods couldn't save from you?"

While he was still speaking, the king asked, "Did we appoint you as one of the king's advisers? Stop talking, or you'll be struck down." The prophet stopped, but first he said, "I know God has decided to destroy you because you've done this and refused to listen to my warning."
After consulting his advisers, King Amaziah of Judah sent a message to King Joash of Israel, son of Jehoahaz and grandson of Jehu: "Come on, let's face each other in battle."

King Joash of Israel sent this reply to King Amaziah of Judah: "A thistle in Lebanon sent word to a cedar in Lebanon, asking for the cedar's daughter as a wife for its son. Then a wild animal from Lebanon came by and trampled the thistle.
You keep telling yourself that you've defeated Edom, and the victory has made you proud and boastful. Stay home. Why stir up trouble that will bring down both you and Judah?"
Amaziah refused to listen. God brought this about to hand Judah over to the enemy, because they had turned to the gods of Edom.
So King Joash of Israel marched up, and he and King Amaziah of Judah faced each other at Beth Shemesh in Judah.
Israel defeated Judah, and the men of Judah fled to their homes.

At Beth Shemesh, King Joash of Israel captured King Amaziah of Judah, son of Joash and grandson of Jehoahaz, and took him to Jerusalem. He tore down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.
He took all the gold and silver and every vessel that was in Obed-Edom's care in God's house. He also seized the palace treasures and took hostages, then returned to Samaria.
King Amaziah son of Joash of Judah lived fifteen years after the death of King Joash son of Jehoahaz of Israel.
The rest of what Amaziah did, from beginning to end, is recorded in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.
From the time Amaziah stopped following the LORD, people in Jerusalem plotted against him. He fled to Lachish, but they sent men after him and killed him there.
They brought his body back on horses and buried him with his ancestors in the City of Judah.
All the people of Judah made sixteen-year-old Uzziah king in place of his father Amaziah.
Uzziah rebuilt Eloth and restored it to Judah after his father died.
Uzziah was sixteen when he became king and ruled fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jechiliah from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, following the example of his father Amaziah.
He sought God during the lifetime of Zechariah, who understood visions from God. As long as Uzziah sought the LORD, God gave him success.
He fought the Philistines and tore down the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod. He built towns around Ashdod and elsewhere in Philistine territory.
God helped him against the Philistines, the Arabs who lived in Gur Baal, and the Meunim.
The Ammonites paid tribute to Uzziah. He grew so powerful that his reputation reached as far as the border of Egypt.
Uzziah built and fortified towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate, and the bend in the wall.

He also built towers in the wilderness and dug many cisterns because he had large herds in the lowlands and on the plains. He loved farming, so he had farmers and vineyard workers in the hills and fertile fields.
Uzziah had an army that went to war in divisions. Jeiel the secretary and Maaseiah the officer drew up the rolls under Hananiah, one of the king's commanders.
There were twenty-six hundred family heads, all brave warriors.
They commanded an army of three hundred seven thousand five hundred trained fighters who helped the king against his enemies.
Uzziah supplied the whole army with shields, spears, helmets, armor, bows, and slingstones.

In Jerusalem, skilled workers made devices for the towers and battlements that could shoot arrows and large stones. Uzziah's fame spread far and wide because he received extraordinary help and became powerful.
Once Uzziah was powerful, pride led him into wrongdoing. He was unfaithful to the LORD his God. He entered the LORD's temple to burn incense on the incense altar.
Azariah the priest went in after him with eighty courageous priests of the LORD.

They confronted King Uzziah and said, "Only the priests descended from Aaron, who have been set apart for this work, may burn incense to the LORD. Leave the sanctuary. You've been unfaithful, and the LORD God won't honor you for this."
Uzziah became furious. He was holding a censer to burn incense, and while he raged at the priests, a serious skin disease broke out on his forehead beside the incense altar in the LORD's house.
Azariah the chief priest and the other priests saw the disease on his forehead and rushed him out. Uzziah himself hurried to leave because the LORD had struck him.
King Uzziah had the skin disease until he died. He lived in a separate house, barred from the LORD's house. His son Jotham took charge of the royal palace and governed the people of the land.
Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, recorded the rest of Uzziah's deeds from beginning to end.
Uzziah died and was buried with his ancestors in the burial field belonging to the kings, because people said, "He had a serious skin disease." His son Jotham became king in his place.
Jotham was twenty-five years old when he became king and ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jerushah daughter of Zadok.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, as his father Uzziah had done, except that he stayed out of the LORD's temple. The people still acted corruptly.
Jotham built the Upper Gate of the LORD's house and did extensive work on the wall of Ophel.
He built towns in Judah's hill country and put up fortresses and towers in the forests.

He fought and defeated the king of the Ammonites. That year the Ammonites paid him a hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat, and ten thousand cors of barley. They paid him the same amount in the second and third years.
Jotham grew powerful because he lived faithfully before the LORD his God.
The rest of what Jotham did, including all his wars and how he lived, is recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
He was twenty-five when he became king and ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem.
Jotham died and was buried in the City of David. His son Ahaz became king in his place.
Ahaz was twenty when he became king and ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem. He failed to do what was right in the LORD's eyes, as his ancestor David had done.
He followed the ways of Israel's kings and cast metal idols for the Baals.
He burned incense in the Valley of Ben Hinnom and burned his children in the fire, following the detestable practices of the nations the LORD had driven out before Israel.
He offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places, on the hills, and under every leafy tree.

So the LORD his God handed him over to the king of Syria. The Syrians defeated him, took many captives, and brought them to Damascus. Ahaz was also handed over to the king of Israel, who inflicted heavy losses on him.
In one day Pekah son of Remaliah killed a hundred twenty thousand brave warriors in Judah because they had abandoned the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
Zichri, a mighty warrior from Ephraim, killed the king's son Maaseiah, the palace administrator Azrikam, and Elkanah, the king's second-in-command.
