The Israelites took two hundred thousand of their own relatives captive, including women, sons, and daughters. They also took a great deal of plunder and carried it to Samaria.

A prophet of the LORD named Oded was there. He went out to meet the army coming into Samaria and said, "The LORD, the God of your ancestors, was angry with Judah and handed them over to you. But you killed them in a rage that has reached heaven.
Now you want to enslave the men and women of Judah and Jerusalem. Don't you have sins of your own against the LORD your God?
Listen to me. Send back the people you've taken captive from your own relatives, because the LORD's fierce anger is on you."
Some leaders of Ephraim confronted the men returning from battle: Azariah son of Johanan, Berechiah son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai.
They told them, "You must keep the captives out of here. What you're doing will make us guilty before the LORD and add to our sins. We're already deeply guilty, and fierce anger hangs over Israel."
So the armed men handed over the captives and plunder before the leaders and the whole assembly.

The men named earlier took charge of the captives. They used the plunder to clothe everyone who had no clothes, gave them sandals, food, and drink, and put oil on them. They set the weak on donkeys and took them to their own people in Jericho, the City of Palms. Then they returned to Samaria.
At that time King Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria for help.
The Edomites had again attacked Judah and taken captives.

The Philistines had also invaded the towns of Judah's lowlands and southern region. They took Beth Shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, and the towns of Soco, Timnah, and Gimzo with their villages, and settled there.
The LORD humbled Judah because of Ahaz, king of Israel, who had run wild in Judah and been deeply unfaithful to the LORD.
King Tilgath-pilneser of Assyria came to Ahaz and added to his troubles instead of helping him.
Ahaz took valuables from the LORD's house, the royal palace, and the officials' houses and gave them to the king of Assyria. It did him no good.
Even in his trouble, this same King Ahaz became more unfaithful to the LORD.

He sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, whose people had defeated him. He said, "The gods of Syria's kings helped them. I'll sacrifice to those gods so they'll help me too." Those gods brought ruin on him and all Israel.
Ahaz gathered the vessels from God's house, cut them to pieces, and shut the doors of the LORD's house. He set up altars for himself on every corner in Jerusalem.
In every town of Judah he built high places to burn incense to other gods. This provoked the anger of the LORD, the God of his ancestors.
The rest of his deeds and how he lived, from beginning to end, are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.
Ahaz died and was buried in Jerusalem, outside the tombs of Israel's kings. His son Hezekiah became king in his place.
Hezekiah was twenty-five when he became king and ruled twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother was Abijah daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, following the example of his ancestor David.
In the first month of his first year as king, he opened the doors of the LORD's house and repaired them.
He called the priests and Levites together in the open area on the east side.
He told them, "Listen, Levites. Set yourselves apart, then set apart the house of the LORD, the God of your ancestors. Take everything unclean out of the holy place.
Our ancestors were unfaithful and did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD our God. They abandoned him, turned away from his dwelling place, and turned their backs on him.
They shut the doors of the porch and put out the lamps. They stopped burning incense and presenting burnt offerings in the holy place to the God of Israel.
That's why the LORD's anger fell on Judah and Jerusalem. As you can see for yourselves, he's made them a source of horror, shock, and scorn.
Our ancestors have fallen by the sword, and our sons, daughters, and wives have been taken captive because of it.
Now I intend to make a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel, so his fierce anger will turn away from us.
My sons, don't neglect your work now. The LORD has chosen you to stand before him, serve him, and burn incense to him."

Then these Levites came forward: from the Kohathites, Mahath son of Amasai and Joel son of Azariah. From Merari's family came Kish son of Abdi and Azariah son of Jehallelel. From the Gershonites came Joah son of Zimmah and Eden son of Joah.
From Elizaphan's family came Shimri and Jeuel. From Asaph's family came Zechariah and Mattaniah.
From Heman's family came Jehuel and Shimei. From Jeduthun's family came Shemaiah and Uzziel.
They gathered their fellow Levites and consecrated themselves. Then they went in to cleanse the LORD's house, following the king's order in keeping with the LORD's words.
The priests went inside the LORD's house to cleanse it. They brought everything unclean they found in the temple out to the courtyard. The Levites took it from there to the Kidron Brook.

They began the work of consecration on the first day of the first month and reached the temple porch on the eighth day. They took eight days to consecrate the LORD's house and finished on the sixteenth day of the month.

Then they went to King Hezekiah in the palace and said, "We've cleansed the entire LORD's house, including the altar for burnt offerings and all its utensils, and the table for the sacred bread and all its utensils.
We've also restored and consecrated all the vessels King Ahaz threw away when he was unfaithful during his reign. They're now in front of the LORD's altar."
King Hezekiah got up early, gathered the officials of the city, and went to the LORD's house.

They brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah. He ordered the priests, Aaron's descendants, to offer them on the LORD's altar.
They slaughtered the bulls, and the priests took the blood and sprinkled it on the altar. They slaughtered the rams and then the lambs, sprinkling their blood on the altar as well.
They brought the male goats for the sin offering in front of the king and the assembly, and those present laid their hands on them.
The priests slaughtered the goats and offered their blood on the altar to make atonement for all Israel. The king had ordered the burnt offering and sin offering to be made for all Israel.

He stationed Levites in the LORD's house with cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps, following the instructions of David, Gad the king's seer, and Nathan the prophet. The command had come from the LORD through his prophets.
The Levites took their places with David's instruments, and the priests stood with their trumpets.
Hezekiah ordered them to present the burnt offering on the altar. As the offering began, the song to the LORD began too, with trumpets and the instruments of King David of Israel.
The whole assembly worshiped, the singers sang, and the trumpets sounded until the burnt offering was complete.
When they finished, the king and everyone with him bowed down and worshiped.
King Hezekiah and the officials told the Levites to praise the LORD with the words of David and Asaph the seer. They sang praises with joy, then bowed their heads and worshiped.

Hezekiah said, "You've consecrated yourselves to the LORD. Come forward and bring sacrifices and thank offerings to the LORD's house." The assembly brought sacrifices and thank offerings, and everyone who was willing also brought burnt offerings.
The assembly brought seventy bulls, a hundred rams, and two hundred lambs, all for burnt offerings to the LORD.
They also consecrated six hundred cattle and three thousand sheep.

There were too few priests to skin all the burnt offerings. Their fellow Levites helped until the work was finished and the other priests had consecrated themselves. The Levites had been more diligent than the priests about consecrating themselves.
There were many burnt offerings, along with the fat of the peace offerings and the drink offerings for each burnt offering. In this way the worship at the LORD's house was restored.
Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced over what God had made possible for them, because it had all come together so quickly.

Hezekiah sent word throughout Israel and Judah, and wrote letters to Ephraim and Manasseh, inviting everyone to come to the LORD's house in Jerusalem to celebrate Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel.
The king, his officials, and the whole assembly in Jerusalem had agreed to celebrate Passover in the second month.
They couldn't celebrate it at the usual time because too few priests had consecrated themselves and the people hadn't gathered in Jerusalem.
The king and the whole assembly agreed that the new date was right.
They issued a decree throughout Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, inviting the people to Jerusalem to celebrate Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel. Few people had been observing it as prescribed.

At the king's order couriers went throughout Israel and Judah with letters from him and his officials. The letters said, "People of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, so that he'll return to those of you who survived the kings of Assyria.
Don't follow the example of your ancestors and relatives. They were unfaithful to the LORD, the God of their ancestors, and he gave them over to devastation, as you can see.
Don't be stubborn like your ancestors. Yield to the LORD, come into the sanctuary he has set apart forever, and serve the LORD your God so his fierce anger turns away from you.

If you return to the LORD, your relatives and children will receive compassion from their captors and come back to this land. The LORD your God is gracious and merciful. He'll welcome you if you return to him."
The couriers went from town to town through Ephraim and Manasseh as far as Zebulun, but people laughed at them and mocked them.
Still, some people from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and went to Jerusalem.
God also united the people of Judah so they obeyed what the king and officials had commanded in keeping with the LORD's word.
A huge crowd gathered in Jerusalem in the second month to celebrate the Festival of Unleavened Bread.
They took down the altars in Jerusalem, including all the incense altars, and threw them into the Kidron Brook.
They slaughtered the Passover lambs on the fourteenth day of the second month. The priests and Levites were ashamed, so they consecrated themselves and brought burnt offerings into the LORD's house.
They took their assigned places according to the law of Moses, the man of God. The priests received the blood from the Levites and sprinkled it.
Many in the assembly hadn't consecrated themselves. The Levites slaughtered the Passover lambs on behalf of everyone who was unclean, to dedicate the offerings to the LORD.

Many people from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun hadn't purified themselves, yet they ate the Passover meal contrary to what was written. Hezekiah had prayed for them, saying, "May the good LORD forgive everyone
who sets their heart on seeking God, the LORD, the God of their ancestors, even if they haven't met the sanctuary's requirements for being clean."
The LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.

The Israelites who had come to Jerusalem celebrated the Festival of Unleavened Bread for seven days with great joy. Every day the Levites and priests praised the LORD with singing and loud instruments.

Hezekiah encouraged all the Levites who showed skill in serving the LORD. The people ate throughout the seven-day festival, presented peace offerings, and made confession to the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
The whole assembly agreed to celebrate for seven more days, and they did so with joy.

King Hezekiah of Judah gave the assembly a thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep for offerings. The officials gave a thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep. A great many priests consecrated themselves.
Everyone from Judah celebrated, together with the priests and Levites, the people who had come from Israel, and the foreigners who had come from Israel or were living in Judah.
Jerusalem was filled with joy. Nothing like it had happened there since the days of Solomon son of David, king of Israel.
Then the Levitical priests stood up and blessed the people. God heard them, and their prayer reached his holy dwelling in heaven.

When the festival was over, the Israelites who had been there went out to the towns of Judah. They smashed the sacred pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and tore down the high places and altars throughout Judah and Benjamin, and also in Ephraim and Manasseh, until they had removed them all. Then they went back to their own towns and property.

Hezekiah assigned the priests and Levites to their divisions, each person with specific duties. They presented burnt offerings and peace offerings, served, gave thanks, and offered praise at the gates of the LORD's sanctuary.

The king set aside part of his own possessions for the daily morning and evening burnt offerings, and for those offered on Sabbaths, at new moons, and at the appointed festivals, as written in the LORD's law.
He ordered the people living in Jerusalem to give the priests and Levites their share so they could devote themselves to the LORD's law.

As soon as the order went out, the Israelites brought generous first portions of grain, new wine, oil, honey, and everything their fields produced. They brought in a tenth of all they had in great abundance.

The people of Israel and Judah who lived in Judah's towns also brought a tenth of their cattle and sheep and a tenth of what had been dedicated to the LORD their God. They piled the offerings in heaps.
They began making the piles in the third month and finished in the seventh.
When Hezekiah and the officials came and saw the heaps, they blessed the LORD and his people Israel.
Hezekiah asked the priests and Levites about the heaps.

Azariah the chief priest, from Zadok's family, answered, "Ever since the people started bringing their offerings into the LORD's house, we've had enough to eat with plenty left over. The LORD has blessed his people, and this great supply is what remains."
Hezekiah ordered them to prepare storerooms in the LORD's house, and they did.
They faithfully brought in the offerings, the tithes, and the dedicated gifts. Conaniah the Levite was in charge, and his brother Shimei was his deputy.

Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath, and Benaiah were supervisors under Conaniah and his brother Shimei. King Hezekiah and Azariah, who was in charge of God's house, had appointed them.
Kore son of Imnah the Levite, the guard at the East Gate, was in charge of the voluntary offerings to God. He distributed the offerings made to the LORD and the most sacred gifts.
Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah served under him in the priests' towns. They were entrusted with giving each division of their fellow priests its share, whatever their rank.

This was in addition to the males three years old and up listed in the family records, including everyone who came into the LORD's house for daily service according to their divisions and assigned duties.
The priests were listed by family, and the Levites twenty years old and up were listed by division and responsibility.
The records also included their little ones, wives, sons, and daughters, everyone in the community. They faithfully kept themselves consecrated for their duties.
In every town, people were appointed by name to give shares to the male descendants of Aaron the priests living on their towns' pasturelands, and to everyone listed in the Levites' family records.
Hezekiah carried this out throughout Judah and did what was good, right, and faithful before the LORD his God.
In everything he undertook to serve God's house and follow the law and commands, he sought his God wholeheartedly and succeeded.
After all these acts of faithfulness, King Sennacherib of Assyria invaded Judah. He camped against its fortified towns, intending to capture them for himself.
Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come and intended to attack Jerusalem.
He consulted his officials and warriors about stopping up the springs outside the city, and they helped him do it.
Many people gathered and stopped up the springs and the stream flowing through the land. They said, "Why should the kings of Assyria come here and find plenty of water?"

Hezekiah took courage, rebuilt all the broken sections of wall, raised them to the towers, and built a second wall outside. He strengthened the Millo in the City of David and made plenty of weapons and shields.
He appointed military commanders over the people, gathered them in the open space at the city gate, and encouraged them.
"Be strong and courageous. Don't be afraid or lose heart because of the king of Assyria or the huge army with him. The one with us is greater than the one with him.
He's relying on human strength, but the LORD our God is with us to help us and fight our battles." The people took heart from what King Hezekiah of Judah said.

After this, King Sennacherib of Assyria sent officials to Jerusalem while he and his army were attacking Lachish. They brought a message to King Hezekiah of Judah and everyone from Judah in Jerusalem:
"This is what King Sennacherib of Assyria says: What are you counting on as you sit under siege in Jerusalem?
Hezekiah tells you, 'The LORD our God will rescue us from the king of Assyria.' Isn't he leading you to die of hunger and thirst?
Didn't this very Hezekiah remove the LORD's high places and altars and order Judah and Jerusalem to worship and burn incense at a single altar?
Don't you know what my ancestors and I have done to the peoples of other lands? Were their nations' gods ever able to save their lands from me?
Which god of any nation my ancestors destroyed could save its people from me? Why would your God be able to save you?
Don't let Hezekiah deceive you or talk you into this. Don't trust him. No god of any nation or kingdom has saved its people from me or my ancestors. Your God has even less chance of saving you."
Sennacherib's officials said still more against the LORD God and his servant Hezekiah.
Sennacherib also wrote letters insulting the LORD, the God of Israel: "The gods of the other nations couldn't rescue their people from me, and Hezekiah's God won't rescue his people either."
The officials shouted in the language of Judah to the people of Jerusalem on the wall. They wanted to frighten and unsettle them so they could capture the city.
They spoke about the God of Jerusalem as if he were one of the gods made by human hands that other peoples worshiped.
Because of this, King Hezekiah and Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, prayed and cried out to heaven.

The LORD sent an angel who struck down the warriors, leaders, and commanders in the Assyrian king's camp. The king returned home in disgrace. When he entered the temple of his god, some of his own sons killed him there with the sword.
So the LORD saved Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem from King Sennacherib of Assyria and from every other enemy, and took care of them on every side.
Many people brought gifts to the LORD at Jerusalem and valuables to King Hezekiah of Judah. From then on, the nations held Hezekiah in high regard.
Around that time Hezekiah became gravely ill and was near death. He prayed to the LORD, who answered him and gave him a sign.
But Hezekiah grew proud and failed to respond fittingly to the kindness he had received. So anger fell on him and on Judah and Jerusalem.
Then Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem humbled themselves over his pride. The LORD's anger didn't come upon them during Hezekiah's lifetime.
Hezekiah enjoyed great wealth and honor. He built treasuries for silver, gold, precious stones, spices, shields, and every kind of valuable vessel.
He built storehouses for grain, new wine, and oil, and provided stalls for livestock of every kind and pens for his flocks.
He also built towns for himself and owned many flocks and herds, because God had given him great wealth.
Hezekiah blocked the upper outlet of the Gihon spring and directed its waters down to the west side of the City of David. He succeeded in everything he undertook.
When officials from Babylon sent envoys to ask about the sign that had taken place in the land, God left Hezekiah on his own to test him and reveal what was in his heart.
The rest of Hezekiah's deeds and his acts of faithfulness are recorded in the vision of Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.
Hezekiah died and was buried on the slope leading to the tombs of David's descendants. All Judah and Jerusalem honored him when he died. His son Manasseh became king in his place.
Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for fifty-five years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, following the detestable practices of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.
He rebuilt the high places his father Hezekiah had torn down. He put up altars for the Baals, made Asherah poles, and bowed down to all the heavenly host and served them.
He built altars inside the LORD's house, even though the LORD had said, "My name will be in Jerusalem forever."
He built altars for the entire heavenly host in both courtyards of the LORD's house.

He made his children pass through the fire in the Valley of Ben Hinnom. He practiced sorcery, divination, and witchcraft and consulted mediums and spiritists. He did a great deal of evil in the LORD's eyes and provoked his anger.
He put the idol he had carved in God's house. God had told David and his son Solomon, "I'll put my name forever in this house and in Jerusalem, which I chose out of all the tribes of Israel.
I'll keep Israel in the land I assigned to your ancestors as long as they carefully do everything I've commanded them, keeping the whole law, the statutes, and the rulings I gave them through Moses."
Manasseh led Judah and Jerusalem astray until they did more evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites.
The LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they refused to listen.
So the LORD brought the Assyrian king's army commanders against them. They seized Manasseh, bound him in chains and shackles, and took him to Babylon.
In his distress, he pleaded with the LORD his God and humbled himself deeply before the God of his ancestors.
He prayed, and God was moved by his plea. God heard him and restored him to his kingdom in Jerusalem. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God.

After that he built an outer wall for the City of David, from west of Gihon in the valley to the entrance of the Fish Gate. He took it around Ophel and built it very high. He also put capable commanders in all Judah's fortified towns.
He removed the foreign gods and the idol from the LORD's house. He took all the altars he had built on the temple hill and in Jerusalem and threw them outside the city.
He restored the LORD's altar, presented peace offerings and thank offerings on it, and ordered Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel.
The people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God.
The rest of Manasseh's deeds, his prayer to his God, and what the seers told him in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel, are recorded in the Acts of the Kings of Israel.

The History of Hozai records his prayer and how God heard him. It also records his sins, his unfaithfulness, and the places where he built high places and set up Asherah poles and carved images before he humbled himself.
Manasseh died and was buried at his own house. His son Amon became king in his place.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king and ruled two years in Jerusalem.
He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, as his father Manasseh had done. Amon sacrificed to all the carved idols his father had made and served them.
Unlike his father Manasseh, Amon refused to humble himself before the LORD and became more and more unfaithful.
His officials plotted against him and killed him in his own house.
The people of the land killed everyone who had plotted against King Amon and made his son Josiah king in his place.
Josiah was eight years old when he became king and ruled thirty-one years in Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes and followed the ways of his ancestor David without turning to the right or left.

In the eighth year of his reign, while he was still young, he began to seek the God of his ancestor David. In his twelfth year he began clearing Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherah poles, and the carved and cast idols.

They tore down the altars of the Baals in front of him. He cut down the incense altars above them and smashed the Asherah poles and the carved and cast idols. He ground them to dust and scattered it on the graves of those who had sacrificed to them.
He burned the bones of the priests on their own altars. In this way he cleansed Judah and Jerusalem.
He did the same in the towns and surrounding ruins of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, as far as Naphtali.
He tore down altars, crushed Asherah poles and carved images to powder, and cut down all the incense altars throughout Israel. Then he went back to Jerusalem.

In the eighteenth year of his reign, after cleansing the land and the temple, he sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the city governor, and Joah son of Joahaz the recorder to repair the house of the LORD his God.

They went to Hilkiah the high priest and handed over the money brought into God's house. The Levite gatekeepers had collected it from Manasseh, Ephraim, the rest of Israel, all Judah and Benjamin, and the people of Jerusalem.
They handed it to the men overseeing work on the LORD's house, who paid the workers to restore and repair it.
The money went to carpenters and builders to buy cut stone and timber for braces and beams in the buildings the kings of Judah had let fall into ruin.

The men worked faithfully. Jahath and Obadiah, Levites from Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam, from Kohath, supervised and directed them, along with other Levites skilled in playing musical instruments.
They oversaw the men who carried loads and directed workers in all kinds of jobs. Some Levites served as scribes, officials, and gatekeepers.
As they brought out the money that had been taken into the LORD's house, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the LORD's Law given through Moses.
Hilkiah told Shaphan the secretary, "I've found the Book of the Law in the LORD's house." He handed the book to Shaphan.
Shaphan took the book to the king and reported, "Your servants are doing everything you assigned them.
They've taken out the money found in the LORD's house and handed it to the supervisors and workers."
Shaphan the secretary added, "Hilkiah the priest gave me a book." Then he read from it to the king.
When the king heard the words of the law, he tore his clothes.
He gave orders to Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Abdon son of Micah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king's servant.

"Go and ask the LORD for me and for those who remain in Israel and Judah about the words in this book. The LORD has poured out great anger on us because our ancestors failed to obey his word and do everything written here."

Hilkiah and the men the king sent went to Huldah the prophet, who lived in Jerusalem's Second Quarter. She was the wife of Shallum son of Tokhath, son of Hasrah, the keeper of the wardrobe. They told her why they had come.
She said to them, "The LORD, the God of Israel, says to tell the man who sent you to me:
'The LORD says: I'm bringing disaster on this place and its people, all the curses written in the book that was read to the king of Judah.
They abandoned me and burned incense to other gods, provoking my anger with everything they made and did. So my anger will be poured out on this place, and nothing will put it out.'
But tell the king of Judah who sent you to ask the LORD, 'The LORD, the God of Israel, says this about the words you heard:
Your heart was tender. When you heard God's words against this place and its people, you humbled yourself before me, tore your clothes, and wept before me. I have heard you, says the LORD.
I'll gather you to your ancestors. You'll go to your grave in peace, and you won't see the disaster I bring on this place and its people.'" They took this message back to the king.
Then the king summoned all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.

He went up to the LORD's house with the men of Judah, the people of Jerusalem, the priests and Levites, and everyone from the least to the greatest. He read aloud every word of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the LORD's house.

The king stood in his place and made a covenant before the LORD to follow him and keep his commands, testimonies, and statutes with all his heart and soul, carrying out the words of the covenant written in the book.
He had everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin stand in support. The people of Jerusalem followed the covenant of God, the God of their ancestors.

Josiah removed every detestable idol from the lands belonging to the Israelites and had everyone in Israel serve the LORD their God. Throughout his life they continued to follow the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
Josiah celebrated Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem. They slaughtered the Passover animals on the fourteenth day of the first month.
He assigned the priests their duties and encouraged them to serve in the LORD's house.

He told the Levites, who taught all Israel and were set apart for the LORD, "Put the holy ark in the house built by Solomon son of David, king of Israel. You won't have to carry it on your shoulders anymore. Now serve the LORD your God and his people Israel.
Get ready by families and divisions, following the written instructions of King David of Israel and his son Solomon.
Take your places in the sanctuary so a group from a Levite family can serve each family division of your fellow Israelites.
Slaughter the Passover lambs, consecrate yourselves, and prepare the offerings for your people according to what the LORD commanded through Moses."
From his own flocks and herds, Josiah gave everyone there thirty thousand lambs and young goats for the Passover offerings and three thousand bulls.

His officials gave willingly to the people, priests, and Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, who oversaw God's house, gave the priests twenty-six hundred animals from their flocks and three hundred cattle for the Passover offerings.

Conaniah, his brothers Shemaiah and Nethanel, and Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, leaders of the Levites, gave the Levites five thousand animals from their flocks and five hundred cattle for the Passover offerings.
When everything was ready, the priests took their places and the Levites lined up by division, as the king had ordered.
They slaughtered the Passover animals. The priests sprinkled the blood the Levites handed them, and the Levites skinned the animals.
They set aside the burnt offerings and distributed them by family so the people could offer them to the LORD as written in the Book of Moses. They did the same with the cattle.
They roasted the Passover animals over the fire as required. They boiled the sacred offerings in pots, kettles, and pans and carried them quickly to everyone.
Afterward the Levites prepared food for themselves and the priests, Aaron's descendants, who were busy presenting the burnt offerings and the fat until nightfall.

The singers from Asaph's family took their places as directed by David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, the king's seer. The gatekeepers stayed at their posts because their fellow Levites prepared food for them.
Everything needed to serve the LORD was ready that day. They celebrated Passover and presented burnt offerings on the LORD's altar as King Josiah had commanded.
The Israelites who were there celebrated Passover and then kept the Festival of Unleavened Bread for seven days.

Israel hadn't celebrated a Passover like that since the days of Samuel the prophet. None of Israel's kings had celebrated one like Josiah did with the priests, the Levites, everyone from Judah and Israel who had come, and the residents of Jerusalem.
This Passover was celebrated in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign.
After Josiah had put the temple in order, King Neco of Egypt marched up to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates. Josiah went out to confront him.

Neco sent messengers to him, saying, "What quarrel do I have with you, king of Judah? I've come to fight the kingdom I'm at war with. God has told me to hurry. God is with me, so don't get in his way, or he'll destroy you."
Josiah refused to turn back. He disguised himself to fight Neco and ignored what God had told him through Neco. He went into battle in the Valley of Megiddo.
Archers shot King Josiah, and he told his servants, "Get me out of here. I'm badly wounded!"
His servants took him out of his chariot, put him in his second chariot, and brought him to Jerusalem. He died and was buried in his ancestors' tombs. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him.

Jeremiah wrote a lament for Josiah. To this day the men and women who sing laments remember Josiah in their songs. They became an established practice in Israel and are recorded in the collection of laments.
The rest of Josiah's deeds and the faithful things he did in keeping with what is written in the LORD's law,
along with everything he did from first to last, are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
The people of the land took Josiah's son Jehoahaz and made him king in Jerusalem in his father's place.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three when he became king and ruled three months in Jerusalem.
The king of Egypt removed him from the throne in Jerusalem and imposed a fine on the land of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold.
The king of Egypt made Jehoahaz's brother Eliakim king over Judah and Jerusalem and changed his name to Jehoiakim. Neco took Jehoahaz away to Egypt.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king and ruled eleven years in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD his God.
King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon came up against him and bound him in shackles to take him to Babylon.
Nebuchadnezzar also took some of the vessels from the LORD's house to Babylon and put them in his own temple there.
The rest of Jehoiakim's deeds, the detestable things he did, and what was found against him are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. His son Jehoiachin became king in his place.
Jehoiachin was eight years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for three months and ten days. He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes.
At the turn of the year King Nebuchadnezzar sent for him and took him to Babylon with the valuable vessels from the LORD's house. He made Jehoiachin's brother Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem.
Zedekiah was twenty-one when he became king and ruled eleven years in Jerusalem.
He did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD his God. He refused to humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke the LORD's words.
He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear an oath by God. He became stubborn and hardened his heart against returning to the LORD, the God of Israel.
All the leading priests and the people became deeply unfaithful. They followed the detestable practices of the surrounding nations and defiled the house the LORD had set apart in Jerusalem.
The LORD, the God of their ancestors, kept sending messengers to warn them because he had compassion for his people and for his dwelling place.
But they mocked God's messengers, despised his words, and laughed at his prophets until the LORD's anger rose against his people and there was no remedy.

So the LORD brought the king of the Chaldeans against them. He killed their young men with the sword in their own sanctuary. He showed no mercy to young men or young women, the elderly or the infirm. God handed them all over to him.
The king took to Babylon every vessel from God's house, large and small, along with the treasures of the LORD's house and the treasures of the king and his officials.
They burned God's house, broke down Jerusalem's wall, set fire to its palaces, and destroyed its valuables.
He took the survivors to Babylon. They served him and his sons until the kingdom of Persia came to power.
This fulfilled what the LORD had said through Jeremiah. The land enjoyed its Sabbaths, resting as long as it lay desolate, until seventy years had been completed.
In the first year of King Cyrus of Persia, the LORD fulfilled his word through Jeremiah by stirring Cyrus to send out a proclamation throughout his kingdom and put it in writing.

"This is what King Cyrus of Persia says: 'The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth. He has charged me with building a house for him in Jerusalem, in Judah. If any of his people are among you, may the LORD their God be with them, and let them go up.'"
